claims.statement: The connection between Crohn's disease and a sugar-rich diet is proved beyond reasonable doubt. Apart from smoking, this is the strongest clue to an environmental etiology of the disease.
claims.evidence_excerpt: Seventeen studies on eating patterns of Crohn's patients prior to diagnosis, conducted across multiple countries and methods. claims.statement: All of these diets work for the same reason: They reduce the amount of fermentable carbohydrates you're eating, which, in turn, gives the overgrown bacteria in your gut less to eat!
claims.evidence_excerpt: Overview of five dietary approaches for SIBO, all converging on fermentable carbohydrate restriction. Sarna observes that "food doesn't cause SIBO" -- dietary triggers are about symptom management, not etiology.

claims.evidence_excerpt: Historical case reports and clinical observations spanning centuries. The Herter and Gee observations are particularly specific about carbohydrate intolerance.

claims.statement: Inflammation in the small intestine can cause malabsorption of nutrients, while inflammation in the large intestine can inhibit the absorption of water and electrolytes.
claims.evidence_excerpt: Standard nutritional physiology. Signs of malnutrition listed: fatigue, light-headedness, paleness, numbness, tingling, bruising, bone/muscle pain, hair loss, muscle cramping, appetite loss, taste/smell changes.

claims.statement: Most people with chronic intestinal disorders also suffer from malabsorption and, consequently, are malnourished.
claims.evidence_excerpt: General knowledge about malabsorption in intestinal disease. The folate-B12 warning reflects the clinical pearl that high folate can mask B12 deficiency hematologically while neurological damage progresses.
